body: MHLW-funded research group on appropriate use and discontinuation of hypnotics + Japanese Society of Sleep Research (JSSR) working group
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Appropriate Use and Discontinuation of Hypnotics (睡眠薬の適正な使用と休薬のための診療ガイドライン)
status: stale (first ed. 25 June 2013, revised 22 Oct 2013; errata page references a 22 July 2014 version; no later edition found)
recommendation: Built around 40 clinical questions running from first treatment through sleep hygiene and CBT, insomnia with other conditions, chronic insomnia, setting a treatment end-point and methods for stopping hypnotics. Recommendations come from evidence where available and expert consensus otherwise, with a parallel set written for patients. The treatment algorithm names an explicit 'end of treatment' and asks doctor and patient to decide together (shared decision-making) whether to aim for tapering/stopping or for 'safe long-term maintenance'.
strength: Grades not seen (full text not read)

citation.authors: Mishima K
citation.title: [Clinical Practice Guideline for the proper use and cessation of hypnotics]

whatWasRead: abstract (Mishima 2015 summary article) + secondary source (web-search summaries of the JSSR PDF); the guideline PDF itself was blocked (connection refused)
notes: The Japanese guideline is the only national one in this set built around stopping hypnotics. It predates the orexin antagonists, so it does not cover suvorexant, lemborexant or daridorexant. A full read is needed for tapering steps and grades. Kazuo Mishima, who led it, declares lecture fees from Eisai, MSD and Takeda in other papers (see the JRS SAS row).

body: Japanese Respiratory Society + MHLW Refractory Respiratory Diseases research group, with Japanese Society of Sleep Research and others
guidelineTitle: Sleep Apnea Syndrome (SAS) Clinical Practice Guidelines 2020
status: current (Japanese version July 2020; listed by Minds July 2021; English version of therapy CQs 2022)
recommendation: 36 clinical questions; the English version gives the treatment and management CQs (CQ16-36). The abstract says health insurance began covering CPAP in 1998 and the number of CPAP users in Japan is 'about to exceed 500,000'. Specific CPAP, oral appliance and surgery wording was not read.

citation.title: Sleep Apnea Syndrome (SAS) Clinical Practice Guidelines 2020

whatWasRead: abstract
conflictsOfInterest: Many panel members declare industry ties: lecture fees, research funds or industry-donated university courses from CPAP makers and suppliers (Philips Japan, ResMed, Teijin, Fukuda Denshi, Fukuda Lifetech) and from hypnotic makers (Eisai, MSD, Takeda). About 16 of 33 authors declare no COI.
numbersToVerify: moderate-to-severe OSA ~20% of adult men, ~10% of postmenopausal women
notes: Needs a full-text read (ScienceDirect) to get CPAP, oral appliance and HSAT wording and grades. Japanese Circulation Society also has a 2023 sleep-disordered breathing guideline (JCS2023), which was not read.

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule (診療報酬), item C107-2 在宅持続陽圧呼吸療法指導管理料
guidelineTitle: FY2026 (令和8年度) fee schedule: home CPAP management fee 2, eligible patients
recommendation: CPAP is covered (fee 2, criterion ウ) when all three hold: (イ) AHI ≥15; (ロ) strong symptoms such as daytime sleepiness or morning headache that disrupt daily life; (ハ) polysomnography shows sleep fragmentation and loss of deep sleep that CPAP normalises. Patients with AHI ≥30 qualify on symptoms (ロ) alone. Before FY2026 the cut-offs were widely given as AHI ≥20 on in-lab PSG or AHI ≥40 on a home (simplified) test, with symptoms.

citation.authors: Knowlety (commercial annotated copy of the MHLW notices)
citation.title: C107-2 在宅持続陽圧呼吸療法指導管理料 (令和8年度)

whatWasRead: secondary source: annotated copy of the official notice (page text read), plus a hospital patient leaflet (Juntendo Shizuoka) for the earlier AHI 40 home test / AHI 20 PSG rule
numbersToVerify: whether FY2026 still distinguishes home test from PSG
notes: A Chuikyo (central insurance council) re-evaluation proposal said to cut AHI '20以上' to '15以上' so the rule matches Japanese, UK and US guidelines. Check against the MHLW 告示/通知 text. Under the old rule the bar was higher than in most countries (AHI 20 on PSG vs 15 elsewhere).

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule, C107-2 notes (4) and (6)
guidelineTitle: FY2026 fee schedule: home CPAP management fee, continuation and usage rules
recommendation: The management fee continues only for patients judged able to keep going after assessing up to the first 2 months of treatment. After the first 3 months at that clinic, the fee cannot be billed if average CPAP use was under 1 hour a day in every one of the previous 3 months (the device-supply add-on can still be billed). An FY2026 clarification says the fee can be billed if any one of the 3 months averaged ≥1 hour/day. The clinic lends the CPAP device to the patient.

whatWasRead: secondary source (annotated copy of official notice and Q&A)
numbersToVerify: <1 hour/day average in all of the prior 3 months
notes: Far looser than the US Medicare (4 h on 70% of nights) or Korean NHIS adherence tests: Japan stops paying only for near-total non-use. A hospital leaflet puts patient cost at about ¥5,000 a month at 30% copay. Rental is billed each month the patient is managed.

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule, C107-2 注3/注4
guidelineTitle: Remote-monitoring add-on and video/phone management for home CPAP
status: current (remote-monitoring add-on created in FY2018; online-management item present in FY2026 version)
recommendation: Clinics meeting the standard can bill a remote-monitoring add-on (150 points per month, up to 2 months, billed at the next in-person visit) when they track usage and AHI through a connected device between visits and give guidance by phone or video. A separate item (209 points, in place of the 240-point fee) covers management through information and communication devices, once symptom improvement has been confirmed face to face after CPAP starts.

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule (psychotropic polypharmacy and long-term prescribing reductions)
guidelineTitle: Medical fee revisions 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018 (and 2020) on hypnotic/anxiolytic prescribing
status: current (rules carried forward; further revision April 2020)
recommendation: Payments to the prescriber are cut for: 3 or more anxiolytics or 3 or more hypnotics in one prescription (2012); this extended in 2014 (to all doctors, not just psychiatrists, per a Japanese secondary source); 3 or more drugs across anxiolytics, hypnotics, antidepressants or antipsychotics (2016); and, from April 2018, prescribing the same benzodiazepine receptor agonist continuously for 12 months or more to patients with anxiety or insomnia.

numbersToVerify: by March 2017: 2.0% of hypnotic patients on 3+ hypnotics vs 8.9% on 3+ BZs
notes: Evidence says the effect was small. Hirano: the share on 3+ drugs fell in each drug class but not for benzodiazepines as a group. Takeshima 2023 (186,535 new users): 'Japanese policies had no statistically significant effect on long-term prescriptions of hypnotics', and starting with an orexin antagonist went with shorter prescriptions (aHR 1.077). Kimura 2026 (PMID 41612793) looked at the April 2020 revision in people aged 50+.

recommendation: In Japan melatonin is a prescription drug. The only approved product, Melatobel granules (2020), is for children: sleep-onset problems in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. No melatonin product is approved for adult insomnia. Adults get the melatonin receptor agonist ramelteon instead.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition) 失眠症诊断和治疗指南（2025版）
recommendation: CBT-I is stressed and recommended as the first-line treatment for insomnia. Its five core parts are sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation and cognitive therapy. It can be given one-to-one (weekly, 30-60 min, 4-8 sessions), in groups of 5-8, or digitally. New additions: mindfulness, circadian support and intensive sleep retraining.
strength: GRADE (1 strong / 2 weak / 3 not recommended; evidence A-D); grade for this item not seen

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition)
recommendation: Drugs should not be the first choice. Use them on top of treating the cause, CBT-I and sleep health education, following the principles 'individualised, as needed, intermittent, adequate dose, short course' (个体化、按需、间断、足量、短疗程). Recommended order: first, orexin antagonists (DORA) together with short- and intermediate-acting benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BZRA); second, other BZRAs or melatonin receptor agonists (ramelteon, tasimelteon, agomelatine); third, sedating antidepressants (only doxepin, mirtazapine and trazodone, with fluvoxamine dropped from the 2017 list). Quetiapine and olanzapine are not recommended for general insomnia, and nor is gabapentin.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition)
recommendation: Has a full traditional Chinese medicine section. Insomnia is treated as 'bu mei' (不寐病) by pattern differentiation (辨证论治), mainly following the National Administration of TCM standard. A table pairs each pattern with herbal formulas, e.g. liver-qi stagnation → Chaihu Shugan San or Xiaoyao San. Combined care is encouraged: CBT-I plus drugs, physical therapy or TCM, or drugs plus TCM or physical therapy.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition)
recommendation: To switch drugs, lower the old one step by step while starting and raising the new one. To cut down, reduce the bedtime dose gradually or move to intermittent use. Avoid stopping suddenly; tapering can take weeks to months. In older adults use fewer drugs, start low and keep courses short.

body: Chinese Thoracic Society (CMA), Sleep Disordered Breathing Assembly
guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Routine screening of the general population is not recommended (1A). Screen high-risk people with symptoms, signs or related conditions, plus surgical candidates and drivers or workers in safety-critical jobs (1A). Use STOP-Bang (1A); Berlin or STOP may also be used (1B). ESS measures sleepiness but must not be used to diagnose. Questionnaires alone must not diagnose OSA (1A). Validated consumer wearables can help people screen themselves but must not replace medical-grade testing (1A). In resource-limited primary care, simplified criteria using history, examination and pulse oximetry may be used (1A).
strength: Chinese grading: 1 = strong, 2 = weak; evidence A/B

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: In-lab polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard (1A) and comes first for complex cases and high-risk jobs. Home testing (HSAT) is recommended for suspected moderate-to-severe uncomplicated OSA, but not for screening people without symptoms or for diagnosing mild OSA (1A). Diagnose with ICSD-3-TR criteria and grade severity mainly by AHI.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: PAP is recommended first-line for moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥15/h) (1A). It may be considered for mild OSA with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, COPD or marked symptoms, and around surgery (1B). Fixed CPAP is the default because it costs less (1A). Auto-PAP is for people who cannot tolerate CPAP or have positional or variable OSA. Pressure titration is recommended before starting; full-night in-lab titration is the gold standard, and split-night or home auto-titration are acceptable for moderate-to-severe OSA (1A).

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Oral appliances are recommended for primary snoring and mild-to-moderate OSA, and as an alternative or add-on for people who cannot tolerate or keep using PAP (1A). Custom-made devices are preferred. Mouth and throat muscle exercises (myofunctional therapy) are recommended as an add-on (1A). Upper-airway surgery may be considered for clear anatomical problems in people who cannot use PAP (1A).

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Drugs are not routine treatment for OSA (1A). For moderate-to-severe OSA with obesity not controlled by diet and exercise, tirzepatide may be considered as an add-on (1A). For daytime sleepiness that remains despite good OSA treatment, solriamfetol or modafinil is recommended (1A). For sleepiness in people who refuse or cannot use standard treatment, solriamfetol is recommended (1A) and modafinil may be considered (2B). For OSA with insomnia (COMISA), short-term non-benzodiazepine hypnotics may be considered under close monitoring or with CPAP (1B); benzodiazepines are not recommended (1A).
strength: 1A (tirzepatide; solriamfetol/modafinil residual EDS); 1A against benzodiazepines in COMISA

Remote diagnosis combining home testing with electronic questionnaires may be considered (2B).

guidelineTitle: Korean Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: Clinicians may consider zolpidem IR (sleep onset), zolpidem CR (onset and maintenance), eszopiclone and zaleplon (onset), triazolam (onset; moderate evidence), low-dose doxepin and trazodone (maintenance), and ramelteon (onset). Each is phrased 'We recommend that clinicians consider using…'. Suvorexant for maintenance is graded Strong (low evidence), even though the text says 'It is not yet utilized in Korea.'

guidelineTitle: Korean Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: Do not use immediate-release melatonin for adult insomnia (weak). Consider prolonged-release melatonin for sleep-maintenance insomnia in people aged 55 or older (weak, low evidence). Do not use doxylamine (strong, low), diphenhydramine or valerian. Teach patients on benzodiazepines or BzRAs during CBT-I to take them at bedtime (weak).

guidelineTitle: NHIS coverage of polysomnography and PAP for OSA (since 1 July 2018)
recommendation: Since July 2018, national insurance pays for PSG and CPAP rental for patients who meet OSA criteria (CPAP prescribed for AHI ≥15, or AHI ≥5 with OSA symptoms or conditions such as sleepiness, disturbed sleep, hypertension, heart disease or past stroke). To keep coverage after the trial period, the patient must use the device ≥4 h a night on ≥70% of 30 consecutive nights (21 days) within the first 3 months.

numbersToVerify: ≥4 h on ≥70% of 30 consecutive nights (21 days) within 90 days
patient pays about 14 USD/month covered vs 1,627-2,033 USD to buy
notes: Same adherence test as US Medicare. Covered patients were more likely to keep using CPAP (p=0.007). Before coverage, Korean adherence was reported at 20-60%. The AHI eligibility above is one hospital's prescribing rule; check it against the HIRA notice.

body: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS)
guidelineTitle: Approval of lemborexant (Dayvigo, Eisai Korea); daridorexant pending
recommendation: MFDS approved lemborexant on 23 June 2026 for 'adult patients aged 18 years and older who have difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep'. For daridorexant, Nxera Pharma Korea has filed for marketing authorisation and expects approval in 2027 (trade press, March 2026).

citation.authors: Son HM (Dailypharm)
citation.title: Eisai Korea's Dayvigo approved by MFDS

whatWasRead: news article (page read)
notes: Korea was among the last major Asian markets without any orexin antagonist; the 2020 guideline said suvorexant was 'not yet utilized in Korea'. No reimbursement information was found.

body: Korean Society of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery + Korean Society of Sleep and Breathing
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline: Clinical Efficacy of Nasal Surgery in the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
recommendation: Ten key action statements on nasal surgery (septoplasty, turbinate, nasal valve, septorhinoplasty, sinus surgery) for OSA, mainly to make PAP more comfortable and improve quality of life: 3 strong recommendations, 3 recommendations and 4 options (ACP grading).

citation.authors: Park DY, Cho JH, Jung YG, et al.
citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Clinical Efficacy of Nasal Surgery in the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea

whatWasRead: abstract
conflictsOfInterest: 'No potential conflict of interest relevant to this article was reported.'
notes: No general Korean adult OSA treatment guideline (PAP, oral appliance) was found; Korea appears to rely on AASM. The only national OSA guideline found is this ENT one.

guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders
status: stale (2017; IPS 2025 guideline cycle did not cover sleep)
recommendation: 'For the short term insomnia, pharmacotherapy is indicated, while for the chronic insomnia, cognitive behavior therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is preferred.' Drugs are 'not routinely recommended for the management of chronic insomnia'. But 'considering the limited availability of trained CBT-I therapist, consensus was reached that in certain circumstances where CBT-I is not possible for any reason, pharmacotherapy may be instituted for long term', citing Z-drug data out to 6 months. A common approach is to start drugs alongside CBT-I and then taper to CBT-I alone.

citation.authors: Gupta R, Das S, Gujar K, Mishra KK, Gaur N, Majid A
citation.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders

whatWasRead: full text
numbersToVerify: CBT-I may stop once sleep is stable ≥4 weeks
notes: The only guideline in this set that openly allows long-term hypnotics because CBT-I therapists are scarce. The authors say Indian research is limited and evidence comes mostly from Western populations. A separate 2024 'expert consensus' on zolpidem (IJRMS) is not an IPS document and was not read.

guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders
recommendation: Melatonin 3 mg tablets are available in India and 'may be used to induce sleep, however, data do not support its efficacy as a hypnotic agent. It is rather used as a chronobiotic.' Ramelteon (8-24 mg/day) and agomelatine (25-50 mg/day) are available. Sedating antidepressants (tricyclics, trazodone, mirtazapine) are for comorbid psychiatric disorders or when BZ/BzRA side effects are not tolerated. Over-the-counter antihistamines have limited efficacy data.

citation.authors: Gupta R, Das S, Gujar K, Mishra KK, Gaur N, Majid A
citation.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders

whatWasRead: full text
notes: The 8-24 mg ramelteon range goes above the 8 mg label dose in the US and Japan. Whether melatonin in India is sold by prescription or over the counter was not checked.

body: Indian Initiative on Obstructive Sleep Apnea (INOSA), under the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014 (First edition)
status: stale (first edition 2014; no second edition found)
recommendation: CPAP is the 'gold standard' for moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI >15) and an option for milder OSA. Treatment is indicated for AHI (or RDI) ≥15/h, or AHI ≥5 but <15 with sleepiness, impaired thinking or mood, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease or past stroke (Evidence Quality A, Strong Recommendation).

citation.authors: Sharma SK, Katoch VM, Mohan A, et al.
citation.title: Consensus and evidence-based Indian initiative on obstructive sleep apnea guidelines 2014 (first edition)

whatWasRead: full text (Lung India reprint; original Indian J Med Res 2014;140:451-68, PMID 25366217)
conflictsOfInterest: 'Source of Support: Nil Conflict of Interest: None declared.'
notes: Typo in the guideline: it defines sleepiness as 'a score of <10 on ESS'; it should read >10. The guideline was written because awareness of OSA among Indian primary-care doctors is described as 'dismally low'.

guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014
recommendation: Home (portable) testing (type 3/4) can be a useful, cost-effective and quick way to diagnose, but must be done only after a full sleep evaluation and with a practitioner qualified to run sleep studies (Evidence Quality B, Recommended). AHI may be falsely low because sleep time is not measured. Type 2 unattended PSG is also recommended (B).

citation.authors: Sharma SK, Katoch VM, Mohan A, et al.
citation.title: Consensus and evidence-based Indian initiative on obstructive sleep apnea guidelines 2014 (first edition)

whatWasRead: full text

guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014
recommendation: Surgery is recommended for patients who failed or cannot tolerate PAP. Bariatric surgery is 'strongly recommended' for obese OSA patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m2 (Evidence Quality B), with a repeat PSG afterwards. Oral appliances, made by sleep-trained dentists, are for snoring or mild-to-moderate OSA. Modafinil and armodafinil are 'the only agents approved' for daytime sleepiness that remains despite adequate PAP (Evidence Quality A, Strong).

citation.authors: Sharma SK, Katoch VM, Mohan A, et al.
citation.title: Consensus and evidence-based Indian initiative on obstructive sleep apnea guidelines 2014 (first edition)

whatWasRead: full text
notes: No national CPAP reimbursement scheme was found for India; patients largely pay out of pocket. This was not verified and needs a source.

guidelineTitle: Restriction on Z-drugs after complex sleep behaviours
recommendation: TFDA 'banned doctors from prescribing medicine containing any of four ingredients' (eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem, zopiclone) to patients who have had sleepwalking or similar movements while partly conscious. Three of the four were already Class IV controlled drugs.

citation.authors: Taiwan News
citation.title: (TFDA bans Z-drug prescribing to patients with complex sleep behaviours)

whatWasRead: news article (page read)
notes: This mirrors the FDA's April 2019 boxed warning. No national Taiwanese insomnia or OSA guideline was found in English or by a quick Chinese search. Taiwan's literature concentrates on zolpidem doctor-shopping (about 24% of insomnia patients in one study) and NHI-database harms.

body: Saudi sleep medicine experts (e-Delphi; Saudi Sleep Medicine Group helped recruit)
guidelineTitle: Using benzodiazepines and Z-drugs for managing primary insomnia in adults in Saudi Arabia: an e-Delphi study to aid the development of clinical guidelines
status: pre-guideline consensus; no national guideline found
recommendation: Over three Delphi rounds (2018; 15, 17 and then 11 experts), 16 statements on benzodiazepine and Z-drug use reached ≥80% agreement for inclusion in future Saudi guidelines; 5 were rejected. The statement texts were not read.

citation.authors: Dobia A, Ryan K, BaHammam AS, Edwards A
citation.title: Using benzodiazepines and Z-drugs for managing primary insomnia in adults in Saudi Arabia: an e-Delphi study to aid the development of clinical guidelines

whatWasRead: abstract
notes: A companion survey (PLoS One 2019, PMID 31398230) asked Saudi physicians about using international insomnia guidelines. No Saudi OSA guideline was found in PubMed.

body: Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE), Ministry of Health
guidelineTitle: (none found)
recommendation: No ACE Clinical Guidance on insomnia or OSA was found; the ACE topics seen include GAD, gout, asthma and osteoporosis. SingHealth education pieces call CBT-I first-line and mention 'stringent regulations of hypnotic agents, such as benzodiazepines' in Singapore.

citation.authors: SingHealth Duke-NUS Sleep Centre
citation.title: What's new in insomnia (primary care)

whatWasRead: secondary source (search summaries; ACE site not opened)
notes: Check the ACE repository (ace-hta.gov.sg) directly. A Singapore MOH clinical practice guideline on prescribing benzodiazepines (thought to be 2008) may apply; it was not found or verified here.

body: World Health Organization, mhGAP (Guidelines for the management of conditions specifically related to stress)
guidelineTitle: WHO guidelines on conditions specifically related to stress
status: stale (2013; the 2023 mhGAP update kept a 'conditions related to stress' module, whose insomnia wording was not checked)
recommendation: For secondary acute insomnia (in the first month after a potentially traumatic event): 'Relaxation techniques and advice about sleep hygiene should be considered for adults' (standard); 'Benzodiazepines should not be offered to adults' (standard); 'Benzodiazepines should not be offered to children and adolescents' (strong).

citation.authors: Tol WA, Barbui C, van Ommeren M
citation.title: Management of acute stress, PTSD, and bereavement: WHO recommendations

whatWasRead: full text of JAMA Viewpoint table (authored by WHO staff); WHO publication page
notes: This is WHO's only formal recommendation about insomnia treatment, and it covers only acute insomnia after trauma. WHO has no chronic insomnia guideline.

body: World Health Organization, Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP)
guidelineTitle: mhGAP guideline (3rd edition, 2023) / mhGAP Evidence Resource Centre
recommendation: Absence finding: mhGAP covers 11 topics (child and adolescent disorders, depression, psychosis and bipolar, epilepsy, dementia, alcohol, self-harm and suicide, drug use, other emotional and bodily distress complaints, conditions related to stress, anxiety). There is no sleep or insomnia module and no OSA content.

citation.authors: WHO
citation.title: mhGAP Evidence Resource Centre

whatWasRead: guideline web page
notes: Not verified: whether the mhGAP Intervention Guide 2.0 (2016) handles sleep problems inside other modules (e.g. depression). It was not read.

body: WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines
guidelineTitle: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (23rd list 2023; 24th list Sept 2025)
recommendation: No hypnotic is listed for insomnia: no Z-drug, orexin antagonist, melatonin or ramelteon. In the mental health section diazepam is listed only for anxiety disorders; in 2023 benzodiazepines for anxiety were limited to diazepam and lorazepam for 'short-term emergency' treatment of acute severe anxiety. Midazolam is listed for procedural sedation and diazepam for palliative care.

citation.authors: Barbui C, Papola D, Todesco B, Gastaldon C, Ostuzzi G
citation.title: Ground-breaking change to the mental health section of the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines: implications for low- and middle-income countries

whatWasRead: secondary source (Wikipedia list of the current EML; abstract/metadata of Barbui 2024; search summary of Papola 2024)
conflictsOfInterest: Barbui et al. wrote 9 of 13 applications to the 24th EML Expert Committee, commissioned and funded by WHO
notes: Check against the official 2025 EML PDF. CPAP devices are not covered by the medicines list; the WHO Priority Medical Devices list was not checked.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
recommendation: Infants: '14–17h (0–3 months of age) or 12–16h (4–11 months of age) of good quality sleep, including naps.' Ages 1-2: '11-14 hours of good quality sleep, including naps, with regular sleep and wake-up times.' Ages 3-4: '10–13h of good quality sleep, which may include a nap, with regular sleep and wake-up times.'

citation.authors: WHO
citation.title: Guidelines on Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour and Sleep for Children under 5 Years of Age

whatWasRead: guideline web page + WHO news release
notes: WHO's only sleep-duration guidance. There is no WHO sleep-duration recommendation for adults or for school-age children (the 2020 physical activity guidelines cover ages 5+ without sleep). Recommendation grades were not seen.

guidelineTitle: ICD-11, Chapter 07 Sleep-wake disorders
recommendation: ICD-11 adds a separate Chapter 7 for sleep-wake disorders and drops ICD-10's split between organic and non-organic sleep disorders. It covers insomnia, hypersomnolence, sleep-related breathing, circadian, sleep-related movement disorders and parasomnias. Chronic insomnia is 7A00 (≥3 months) and short-term insomnia 7A01 (<3 months); obstructive sleep apnoea is 7A41.

citation.authors: Spiegelhalder K, Riemann D
citation.title: Sleep disorders: comparison of ICD-11 and ICD-10

whatWasRead: secondary source (search snippets of the review and ICD-11 code sites; WHO ICD browser not readable)
notes: Confirm the codes in the WHO ICD-11 browser.

guidelineTitle: (none found)
recommendation: Absence finding: WHO has no guideline on diagnosing or treating obstructive sleep apnoea, and none on chronic insomnia in adults. Its sleep-related outputs are the 2013 stress guideline (acute insomnia after trauma), the 2019 under-5 sleep durations, the EML (no hypnotics) and ICD-11 Chapter 7.
whatWasRead: guideline web pages (mhGAP evidence centre, WHO publication pages) + searches
notes: This absence is itself a finding for the dataset: international OSA and insomnia standards come from professional societies (AASM, ESRS, ERS, World Sleep Society), not WHO.
